attrs.evidence: R6 shipped two readings and made the permissive one primary. GPT-5.6 ruled that neither endpoint is the assurance reading and gave the reason for each. `eliminative` is too permissive: it treats an identified-but-uninvestigated doubt as no attack at all, so DEF-1PA-REDUCTION-MISMATCH read as eliminated while the elimination argument's own open doubt sat unaddressed — and Assurance 2.0 is explicit the other way, that an undeveloped defeater leaves the node it attacks unsupported until the doubt is resolved. `strict` is too aggressive: it makes a deliberately TERMINATED accepted-risk doubt behave like an unresolved blocking attack, so DEF-SUBSTRATE-MISEXECUTION would defeat every argument resting on ASM-SUBSTRATE-INTEGRITY and the point of termination disappears. The middle state is what this loop has been circling since R5: AN IDENTIFIED DOUBT IS NEITHER A PROVED COUNTERARGUMENT NOR IRRELEVANT METADATA. All three readings are computed on every run and their pairwise disagreements are printed.
attrs.prior_art: GPT-5.6's audit of INV-R6 §2. Bloomfield, Netkachova & Rushby, Assurance 2.0 (arXiv:2405.15800) on undeveloped defeaters leaving a node unsupported. Modgil & Prakken on ASPIC+, where a preference ordering is what turns an attack into a defeat.
attrs.statement: The assurance-state candidate reading is `active_unresolved`: an open or sustained doubt is an active challenge to what it attacks; an eliminated doubt is inactive; a terminated doubt is residual risk carried under policy and not an attack. It is a candidate, not a ruling, and it has no promotion authority.
